Objectives:
RESOURCE OBJECTIVES
1.To remove sagebrush from 50-70% of the target area, creating a
mosaic of sage stands and grass/forb meadows.
2.To increase forage production by 100% within 2 years through
post-burn seeding with native species.
3.To improve the vigor and biological diversity of native grasses
and forbs.
4.To improve watershed condition by improving ground cover by
100% within 2 years.
5.To improve spring, fall, and winter range condition for mule
deer.
6.To compare prescribed burning treatments with herbicide and
dixie harrowing treatments in similar sage stands.
PRESCRIBED FIRE OBJECTIVES
1.Minimum flame lengths of 4 feet over 40% of the area.
3.Minimum flame lengths of 1 foot over an additional 20% of the
area.
4.Reduce total fuel loading by 75% over 50% of the area.
5.Keep all slop-overs occurring outside the allowable area less
then 20 acres.
6.Manage the fire for safety and cost effectiveness.
TOLERABLE DEVIATION OF OBJECTIVES
1.To remove 40-80% of the sagebrush from the target area.
2.To improve watershed condition and increase forage production
by 80-200% within 3 years.
3.Minimum flame lengths of 2 feet over 30-50% of the area.
4.Minimum flame lengths of 6 inches to 2 feet over an additional
10-30% of the area.
Planned_Implementation:
The third 95 acre sub-area will be treated with prescribed fire. The fire will be planned in the
spring so that the potential for the fire running into surrounding PJ is limited. Grazing will be
deferred prior to the planned burn to preserve fine fuels. The objective will be to patch burn and
top kill sagebrush by approximately 60% in half of the sub-area. It is expected that forage
production will increase by 100%.
Actual_Implementation:
The burn was started around 1200 with
blacklining along the northeastern end of the burn. Several
narrow strips were run east/ west. Wind speeds were low, spread
was minimal and holding action along this edge was not needed .
Everything north of the dirt tank was ignited by 1300 and
ignition moved to the larger area south of the dirt tank.
Minimal blacklining was done on exposed boundaries on this
portion of the burn and narrow strips were used for main
ignition. Twice throughout the burn I tried to increase strip
width when fuel or wind conditions seemed to improve but had to
revert back to narrow widths when spread did not occur. Ignition
continued with 4-10 ignition personnel throughout the afternoon
with east / west strips from 10-25 feet wide. A small slopover on
the eastern side of the burn torched several pinyon/ juniper and
spotted 1-2 chains into adjacent 1000 hour fuels but did not
spread above the low slope; minimal holding action was needed on
that slopover. The burn was completed at 1800.
Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
1)To remove sagebrush from 50-70% of the target areas, creating a
mosaic of sage stands and grass/forb meadows (tolerable of 40-
80%). Due to minimal spread sage was only removed over 20-30% of
the area, generally in pockets where conditions (wind, fuel
moisture, growth form, understory grasses) were somehow
different. This objective was not met.
2)To increase forage production by 100% within 2 years through
post-burn seeding with native species (tolerable of 80-100%).
Unknown but good potential for seeded species to respond well in
openings. I would expect that forage production would increase
across the stand by 70-80%, simply because there was little
understory in the pre-burn stand. This objective was marginally
met.
3)To improve the vigor and biological diversity of native grasses
and forbs. Unknown but fair potential for native, on-site
species to respond in the small openings. However, the openings
are probably too small and too infrequent for really good vigor
and biological diversity of native on-site species. This
objective was marginally met.
4)To improve watershed condition by improving ground cover by
100% within 2 years (tolerable of 80-100%). See 2 above,
however, the patches are too infrequent, too small, and often in
the wrong locations to enhance watershed to any large degree.
This objective was probably not met.
5)To improve spring, fall, and winter range condition for mule
deer. There will be a definite improvement of these range
conditions but not to the extent that could have been achieved
with a more continues burn. This objective was marginally met.
6)To compare prescribed burning treatments with herbicide and
dixie harrowing treatments in similar sage stands. This burn was
not an effective burn because it did not meet the objectives of
the burn. The prescription needs to be a little drier, hotter,
and windier to be more effective. Comparison would not be
accurate. This objective was not met.
7)Minimum flame lengths of 4 feet over 40% of the area and 1 foot
over an additional 20% of area (tolerable of 2 feet over 30-50
and 6 inches to 2 feet over an additional 10-30%). Flame lengths
were in the appropriate range (2-4 feet in shrubs and 6 inches in
understory) but the amount of spread was not sufficient to meet
the resource objectives. This objective was marginally met.
8)Reduce fuel loading by 75% over 50% of the area. In isolated
areas fuels were reduced by 75% but generally this occurred on
only about 30% of the entire area. A fire in the future would
carry through the majority of the stand with only 2 or 3
locations were spread would be reduced or stopped. This
objective was marginally met.

areas will be broken down along major drainages with an overall goal of treating 500 acres per
year for the next 5 years. Approximately 4400 acres of Forest Service lands will be burned in
conjunction with adjacent BLM lands. The burn will be conducted in the spring to maintain
safety and achieve burn objectives.

Planned_Implementation:
For Unit A (441 acres) a spot ignition technique will be utilized to create 1 - 20 acre openings in  the continuous canopy targeting sub-mature and regeneration PJ. Fire will not be introduced into mature open stands of PJ but will not be excluded from those stands. Broadcast burning would be conducted in the areas with heavy slash and sawdust piles that remain from a commercial wood cutting operation in the late '70s and 80&$s. Black lining would be conducted along the transition between the unit and Unit B to create an adequate buffer for the fall treatment of the unit. This unit would be scheduled for treatment in spring when soil and fuel moisture is too high to promote continuous crown fire.
For Unit B (948 acres) broadcast burning will be conducted to achieve resource objectives. For This unit the objective is to limit mortality of perennial bunch/sod grasses and forbs to 10-15% and kill 80-100% of P J trees to remove vantage positions for predators, reduce tree encroachment into sage parks, and to retain valuable forage and cover species for sage-grouse.
Total acreage consumed by fire would likely be limited to 60 - 90% of the targeted areas. Fire will not be intentionally introduced to, but will not be excluded from, parcels of sagebrush relatively free of PJ encroachment. Retaining well dispersed tracts of unburned sagebrush within the project&$s perimeter would be advantageous as a seed source that would ultimately accelerate re-establishment of sagebrush cover for grouse. This unit would be scheduled for treatment in
late summer/early fall after burning is complete in the PJ unit and when in prescription as detailed in the approved burn plan.

Objectives:
The objectives of the burn were as follows: 
1. Improve forage production of the seeding by accomplishing a 90
percent kill of pinyon-juniper trees and some sagebrush by prescribed
burning. This would change the vegetative composition to
favor grasses (particularly crested wheatgrass) and forbs, and
thereby extend the useful life of the crested wheatgrass seeding.
2. Improve livestock distribution by burning slash piles of downed
trees that were restricting livestock movement.
3. Reduce hazardous wild fire fuels by burning slash piles.
Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
All three of the objectives listed in the fire plan were met. Slash   
piles were completely eliminated to improve livestock distribution and
reduce hazardous fire fuels. A 90 percent kill of trees and shrubs was 
probably not met. However, an estimated 75 percent of these species
were killed, which is considered an excellent kill in this type of 
vegetation. Tree survival was higher along rims where fuel was sparse 
and in areas with a higher big sagebrush density. The tree kill was
also less on the backfired areas. An unburned strip (30 yards wide) was
left along 95 percent of the rim. There were several spots where the
fire jumped the backfire line and burned to the rim .

Trt_Concerns_Desc: The overall goals of this fuels management project are to improve and protect public health and safety and to reduce the threat of stand-replacing wildland fire. The vegetation in the area of the proposed action has been determined to be in Condition Class III (CC3), mixed Fire Regime I and II. In CC3 areas, fire regimes and vegetation attributes have been substantially altered from their natural/historical range and the risk of losing key ecosystem components is high. In the event of wildland fire, dramatic effects can be expected in CC3 areas including fire size, intensity, severity, and/or landscape patterns. In the event of a wildland fire in or around the Price Canyon Recreation Area, flammability of the existing dense vegetation would create a safety hazard, and could pose a threat to the public who use the recreation area as well as to firefighters attempting to control a fire.

Objectives:
The Chaffee Prescribed Burns are designed primarily to enhance wildlife habitat in and
around the Billy Creek State Wildlife Area. Secondary objectives include reducing fuels
to prevent catastrophic fire in the area and restoring more natural vegetation mosaics
throughout the area. Specific objectives of the burn include creating a variety of seral
stages in mountain shrub communities, creating and maintaining earlier seral stages in
pinyon/juniper vegetation types, and reducing dead fuel loadings resulting from previous
mechanical treatments.
Primary concerns of this burn include hunter and visitor safety within and adjacent to the
Billy Creek State Wildlife Area. Other concerns include both enhancing and protecting
valuable big game habitats in this important wildlife/hunting area, protecting private
property and structures within and adjacent to the Project Area, safety of both the public
and fire personnel, and smoke impacts along the Highway 550 corridor.

Goals include:
1 )reducing hazardous wildland fuels and the potential for a catastrophic fire within the vicinity of the
project area,
2)improve wildlife habitat, and
3)maintain or achieve the public land health standards.

Resource Objectives:
Mountain Shrub Unit:
1)Burn approximately 40-60% of the unit in patches 5-20
acres in size
2)As able, orient burned patches and remaining leave strips
uphill to maintain connectivity between the riparian/irrigated
and upland habitats
3)Create openings in the mountain shrub and PJ vegetation
types for regeneration of grasses and forbs
4)Rejuvenate portions of the mountain shrub community
Mechanical Units:
1)Create early and early-mid seral conditions to maintain the
grass/forb and grass/forb/shrub communities on the
landscape for an extended period of time.
2)Reduce remaining slash from hydroaxe and chaining
treatments by 60%
3)Remove 60-80% of the re-encroaching pinyon-juniper
from the mechanically treated areas

Prescribed Fire Objectives:
1)Manage the fire safely and cost-effectively
2)Keep fire within the target units on 80% of the units and
within the Project Area 100% of the time
3)Do not construct prep line or ignite within 200' of Billy
Creek, minimize line construction within this area unless
absolutely necessary to stop fire spread in riparian.
4)Do not intentionally ignite older growth PJ near bottom of
the Mountain Shrub Unit, backing fire into these areas may be
okay, dependent on fire effects
5)Protect facilities within the Billy Creek State Wildlife Area
Planned_Implementation:
Prescribed fire would be implemented in an approximately 485 acre burn unit, which is
characterized by mid- to late-seral mountain shrub and pinyon-juniper. The objective is to burn
approximately 40-60% of the burn unit to create patches 5-20 acres in size. If possible, these
patches would be oriented uphill with leave strips between them so that connectivity between the
Billy Creek drainage and the uphill vegetation is maintained. Tills portion of the project would
create openings for regeneration of grasses and forbs to improve elk habitat, and would also
rejuvenate portions of the mountain shrub community to improve deer habitat. No fire-line
construction is anticipated on tills unit due to good natural barriers; however, small lengths of
hand line or A TV plow line could be constructed in strategic locations based on further field
analysis.
